title: Tenths
keyIdea: Cut one whole into 10 equal parts and each part is one tenth, written 1/10. Ten tenths make 1 whole, so 10/10 = 1. You can count up and down in tenths on a number line, and sharing 3 things between 10 people gives each person 3/10.

kid: Take a bar of chocolate. Cut it into 10 parts that are all the same size. Each part is one tenth. We write it 1/10.
The bottom number tells you how many equal parts the whole has. Here it is 10. The top number tells you how many parts you have. 3/10 means 3 of the 10 parts.
Parts must be the same size. If some are big and some are small, they are not tenths, even if there are 10 of them.
You can count in tenths: 1/10, 2/10, 3/10, and on. When you get to 10/10, you have the whole bar. So 10 tenths make 1 whole.
adult: The English national curriculum for Year 3 asks pupils to 'count up and down in tenths' and to 'recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and in dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10'. Year 4 then writes tenths as decimals, so 3/10 becomes 0.3. In the US, tenths appear in Grade 3 fractions and again in Grade 4, where 4.NF.C.6 links them to decimal notation.

A tenth is one of ten equal parts of a whole. The denominator, 10, names the size of each part. The numerator counts how many parts you have. On a number line from 0 to 1 there are ten equal steps of 1/10, so 10/10 lands on 1. Dividing by 10 makes tenths: 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10, because each of the 3 wholes gives every person one tenth.

Common mistakes: adding the bottoms as well as the tops, so 4/10 + 1/10 becomes 5/20; calling parts tenths just because there are 10, even when they are unequal; mixing up a tenth with ten or with a hundredth; and writing 9/11 for the step after 9/10. Be careful with 12 tenths: it is more than 1 whole. Swap 10 tenths for 1 whole to get 1 and 2/10.

In the lab your child shades a bar one tenth at a time up to 10/10, judges which bars are fairly cut into tenths, hops a frog along a 0 to 1 line in tenths, shares 1, 3 and 7 bars between 10 children, and builds numbers from wholes and tenths, swapping 10 tenths for 1 whole.

familyTip: Line up 10 coins or pasta pieces as one whole. Take some away and say the tenth out loud: 'seven tenths left'. Then add them back one by one: 'eight tenths, nine tenths, ten tenths, one whole'.

visual.caption: The bar is cut into 10 equal parts. Shade some and read the fraction in tenths.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: shade tenths up to 1 whole, judge fair tenths, hop on a 0-1 line, share bars between 10, and swap 10 tenths for 1 whole.

practice.prompt: A bar is cut into 10 equal parts. {a} parts are shaded. How many tenths are not shaded?
practice.hint: The whole bar is 10 tenths. Take away the shaded parts.
practice.explain: The whole is 10/10. {a}/10 are shaded, so 10 − {a} = {=10-a} tenths are not shaded: {=10-a}/10.

practice.prompt: How many tenths are there in {a} wholes?
practice.hint: Each whole is 10 tenths. Count in tens.
practice.explain: Each whole is 10 tenths, so {a} wholes are {a} × 10 = {=a*10} tenths.

practice.prompt: {a}/10 + {b}/10 = ?/10. What is the missing top number?
practice.hint: The parts are all tenths, so the bottom stays 10. Add the tops.
practice.explain: {a} tenths and {b} tenths make {=a+b} tenths, so the answer is {=a+b}/10. The bottom stays 10 because the parts are still tenths.

practice.prompt: Which one is the same as 1 whole?
practice.hint: How many tenths fill the whole bar?
practice.explain: 10/10 means all 10 of the 10 equal parts, which is the whole bar. 1/10 is just one part, and 10/100 is also one tenth.

pool.prompt: A frog is on {a}/10 on a number line. It hops on {b} more tenths. It lands on ?/10. What is the top number?
pool.hint: Each hop adds 1 tenth. Count on from {a}.
pool.explain: Start at {a}/10 and count on {b} tenths: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}, so the frog lands on {=a+b}/10.

pool.prompt: {a} bars are shared fairly between 10 children. Each child gets ?/10 of a bar. What is the top number?
pool.hint: Cut each bar into 10. Each child gets 1 part from each bar.
pool.explain: Each bar is cut into 10 tenths and every child takes one tenth from each of the {a} bars, so each child gets {a}/10. That is {a} ÷ 10.

pool.prompt: A bar is cut into 10 parts. When is each part one tenth?
choices: When all 10 parts are the same size
pool.hint: Think about fair shares. Do the parts need to match?
pool.explain: Tenths are 10 equal parts. If the parts are different sizes they are not tenths, even when there are 10 of them.

pool.hint: Add the tops. The parts are still tenths.
pool.explain: 9 tenths and 1 tenth make 10 tenths, and 10/10 is 1 whole. Adding the bottoms to get 10/20 is a common slip.

pool.hint: Swap 10 tenths for 1 whole. How many tenths are left?
pool.explain: 10 of the tenths make 1 whole, and 7 tenths are left, so 17 tenths is 1 whole and 7/10.

pool.prompt: Count back in tenths: 6/10, 5/10, … What comes next?
pool.hint: Counting back changes the top number. What happens to the bottom?
pool.explain: Each step takes away 1 tenth, so the top goes down by 1 and the bottom stays 10: 4/10.

pool.prompt: Which is more of the same bar: 3/10 or 7/10?
pool.hint: The parts are the same size. Which has more parts?
pool.explain: Both are tenths, so the parts are the same size. 7 parts is more than 3 parts, so 7/10 is more.
